facts.fact: The Pallavas and the Chalukyas were the leading southern dynasties of the post-Gupta period.
Simhavishnu defeated the Kalabhras and began the rule of the imperial Pallavas.
The Pallava core region covered south Andhra Pradesh and north Tamil Nadu.
The Pallava capital was Kanchipuram (Kanchi).
The Pallavas fought the Chalukyas of Vatapi in the north and the Cholas and Pandyas in the south.
Kanchi became an important temple town and hub of trade and commerce.
Pallava kings took titles like Dharma-Maharaja.
Early Pallava king Shivaskandavarman issued the Prakrit Mayidavolu plates, found in Guntur (Andhra Pradesh).
Early Pallava charters were in Prakrit; later ones in Sanskrit and Tamil, written in the Pallava Grantha script.
Simhavishnu ruled c. 575–590 CE.
Simhavishnu took the title Avanisimha ('Lion of the Earth').
Simhavishnu patronised the poet Bharavi, author of the Kiratarjuniya.
Mahendravarman I ruled c. 600–630 CE.
Mahendravarman I took the titles Mattavilasa and Chitrakarapuli ('tiger among painters').
Mahendravarman I was also called Vichitrachitta and Gunabhara.
Mahendravarman I wrote the Sanskrit satire Mattavilasa Prahasana.
Mahendravarman I introduced the Mahendra style of rock-cut architecture.
Mahendravarman's Mandagapattu inscription records a temple made without brick, timber, metal or mortar.
Mahendravarman I was converted from Jainism to Shaivism by the Nayanar saint Appar.
Pulakeshin II defeated Mahendravarman I at the Battle of Pullalur.
The source says Mahendravarman was killed at Pullalur; standard references say he survived and Pallava records claim the victory.
Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla) ruled c. 630–668 CE.
Narasimhavarman I is regarded as the greatest Pallava king.
Narasimhavarman I took the title Vatapikonda ('Conqueror of Vatapi').
Narasimhavarman I defeated Pulakeshin II and destroyed Vatapi.
Pulakeshin II died in 642 CE when Narasimhavarman I captured Vatapi.
Mamalla ('great wrestler') was Narasimhavarman I's title and gave Mamallapuram its name.
Narasimhavarman I founded Mahabalipuram and began the Seven Rathas.
Narasimhavarman I invaded Sri Lanka twice to help the exiled prince Manavamma.
Narasimhavarman I hosted Hsuen Tsang at Kanchipuram in 642 CE.
The great relief 'Arjuna's Penance' (Descent of the Ganga) at Mahabalipuram belongs chiefly to Narasimhavarman I's time.
Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha) ruled c. 695–722 CE.
Rajasimha's reign was marked by peace and a halt to the Chalukya wars.
Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha) built the Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram.
Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha) built the Kailashnath Temple at Kanchipuram.
Rajasimha sent embassies to China.
The Sanskrit writer Dandin, author of the Dashakumaracharita, lived at the Pallava court of Rajasimha.
Nandivarman II ruled c. 736–796 CE.
Nandivarman II built the Vaikunth Perumal Temple, dedicated to Vishnu.
Nandivarman II promoted the Bhakti movement and strengthened village autonomy.
Mahendra style: rock-cut temples using no brick or wood; mandapas were pillared verandas with a garbhagriha.
Mahendra-style examples: Mamandur monuments, Trimurti Mandapa, Mahendravishnu Mandapa.
Mamalla style: monolithic rathas alongside mandapas, with lion-headed pillars.
Mamalla-style examples: Seven Rathas, Varaha Mandapa, Mahishasura Mandapa.
Rajasimha style: elaborate structural temples with intricate carvings.
Rajasimha-style examples: Shore Temple, Kailashnath Temple, Mukunda Temple.
Nandivarman style: smaller, less decorative temples showing decline (Mukteshwar, Matangeshwar).
The four Pallava styles in order are Mahendra, Mamalla, Rajasimha and Nandivarman.
Pallava temples mark the birth of the Dravidian style with a pyramidal vimana.
The Shore Temple has three shrines dedicated to Shiva and Vishnu.
The Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1984).
The Kailashnath Temple has a 16-sided Shivalinga.
The Kailashnath Temple is ringed by 58 mini-shrines (devakulikas).
The Seven Rathas include the Draupadi, Dharmaraja and Bhima Rathas.
The Vaikunth Perumal Temple shows Vishnu standing, sitting and reclining.
Vaikunth Perumal inscriptions record Nandivarman's rise to power.
The Chittannavasal (Sittanavasal) frescoes are cited for Pallava painting; standard references credit them to Jain patrons under the Pandyas.
The Pallava state was a monarchy.
The Pallava empire was divided into Kottams governed by royal officers.
Villages were self-governing, run by assemblies such as the Sabha and the Urar.
Each village had a court called the Dharmasasana.
Kanchi had a ghatika, a Brahmanical centre of learning, where the Kadamba founder Mayurasharman came to study.
Land revenue was the main source of Pallava income.
Taxes were levied on professions, marriages, salt, textiles and cattle.
Agriculture was prosperous and labourers were paid in kind; Hsuen Tsang noted the fertile land.
Brahmadeya villages were tax-free lands given to Brahmins.
Barter prevailed at first; the Pallavas later introduced gold and silver coins.
Merchant guilds were called Manigramam.
Eripatti (tank lands) were lands whose revenue maintained village tanks.
Devadana was land granted to temples.
Pallava kings supported Saivism and Vaishnavism while Buddhism and Jainism declined.
The Alvars were Tamil devotees of Vishnu.
The Nayanars were Tamil devotees of Shiva.
Tradition counts 12 Alvars and 63 Nayanars.
Andal was the only woman among the Alvars.
The Tevaram hymns of Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar form part of the Shaiva Tirumurai.
The Nalayira Divya Prabandham (4,000 hymns of the Alvars) and the Tirumurai are key Bhakti works.
Adi Shankaracharya reinforced Advaita philosophy, reducing Buddhist and Jain influence.
Villages functioned as self-sufficient republics with diverse professional communities.
Pallava kings patronised Sanskrit scholars.
Pallava-era instruments included the Yaazhi, Mridhangam and Murasu.
Constant wars with the Chalukyas of Vatapi and the Pandyas of Madurai drained Pallava strength.
The Chalukyan army invaded and plundered Kanchipuram.
Chalukya Vikramaditya II took Kanchi but spared it and made gifts to the Kailashnath Temple.
The last Pallava king Aparajitavarman was defeated by the Chola king Aditya I in the late 9th century.
Aparajitavarman had earlier won the Battle of Sripurambiyam (c. 885 CE) against the Pandyas.
The Pallavas' fall ushered in Chola dominance in South India.
The Chalukyas of Badami had their capital at Vatapi (Badami) in Karnataka.
Pulakeshin I founded the Badami Chalukya dynasty, fortified Vatapi and performed the Ashvamedha.
Pulakeshin I fortified Vatapi in 543 CE.
Mangalesha, uncle of Pulakeshin II, excavated the Vaishnava cave (Cave 3) at Badami.
Pulakeshin II ruled c. 610–642 CE.
Pulakeshin II checked Harshavardhana on the Narmada.
Pulakeshin II took the title Dakshinapatheshvara ('lord of the south').
The Aihole inscription was composed by the Jain court poet Ravikirti.
The Aihole inscription is on the Meguti Jain temple and is dated 634 CE.
The Aihole inscription is a prashasti of Pulakeshin II.
The Aihole inscription mentions the poets Kalidasa and Bharavi.
Pulakeshin II exchanged embassies with the Sasanian emperor Khusrau II.
A Persian embassy is depicted in an Ajanta Cave 1 mural.
The Badami Chalukyas kept a navy of about 100 ships.
Chalukya administration was centralised, unlike Pallava and Chola village autonomy.
Hiuen-Tsang visited and praised Pulakeshin II's kingdom.
Pulakeshin II made his brother Kubja Vishnuvardhana ruler of Vengi, founding the Eastern Chalukyas of Andhra.
Vikramaditya I, son of Pulakeshin II, restored Chalukya power and recovered Vatapi.
The Rashtrakuta Dantidurga overthrew the last Badami Chalukya, Kirtivarman II, c. 753 CE.
Chalukya temple groups stand at Badami, Aihole and Pattadakal.
The Vesara style, developed by the Chalukyas, blends the Nagara and Dravidian idioms.
Aihole is called the 'cradle of Indian temple architecture'; its temples include the Lad Khan and Durga temples.
Queen Lokamahadevi built the Virupaksha temple at Pattadakal to mark Vikramaditya II's victory over the Pallavas.
Pattadakal has both Nagara (Papanatha) and Dravida (Virupaksha) style temples.
Pattadakal is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1987).
Badami has four rock-cut cave temples, three Hindu and one Jain.
